# `assumed-concurrency`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: correctness · Profile: none · Default: warning · Fixes: none · Options: none

Reports `std.Io` `concurrent` calls whose `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable` is
discarded with `catch unreachable`.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

`io.concurrent`, `Group.concurrent` and `Select.concurrent` promise that the
task runs concurrently with the caller, so they fail with
`error.ConcurrencyUnavailable` when the `Io` implementation cannot keep that
promise: a single-threaded `Io` (`Io.Threaded.init_single_threaded`, or any
`-fsingle-threaded` build), a concurrency limit that is reached, or no thread
or memory left to start the task. That is a condition of the environment the
program runs in, not a programming error, so `catch unreachable` turns an
ordinary resource limit into illegal behavior: a panic in safe builds and
undefined behavior in unsafe ones.

## When it fires

It reports `catch unreachable` directly after `io.concurrent(function, args)`,
after `group.concurrent(io, function, args)` whose first argument is an `Io`,
and after `select.concurrent(.field, function, args)` on a local `Io.Select`.
Propagate the error with `try`, fall back to doing the work another way, or
use `async`, which cannot fail because it may run the task before returning
(only when the task does not need to run alongside the caller).

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn work() void {}

fn start(io: std.Io) void {
    var pending = io.concurrent(work, .{}) catch unreachable;
    pending.await(io);
}
```
